FOR CLAT 2027
Z—

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• On 19 June 2026, the Supreme Court in a landmark judgment
  declared the freedom to walk on demarcated and well-maintained
  footpaths as a fundamental right under Article 21 of the
  Constitution.

• The bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Atul S.
  Chandurkar held that the right to walk on footpaths shall
  override the privilege of a motorised vehicle.

• The Court also urged the government to frame a law to bring this
  right into effect and hold officials accountable for violations.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


Background –

• Pedestrian deaths in India have more than doubled in 10 years,
  now accounting for the second-highest share of road
  fatalities after two-wheeler users.

• The number of pedestrians killed in road accidents rose from 13,894
  in 2015 to 36,526 in 2024 – an increase of nearly 163%.

• Total road fatalities increased by only 21.24% during the same
  period, making the surge in pedestrian deaths particularly
  alarming.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• The share of pedestrian deaths in total road fatalities more than
  doubled from 9.5% in 2015 to 20.61% in 2024.

• This means that one in five road deaths in India is now a
  pedestrian.

• Pedestrian fatalities continued to rise even during the Covid-19
  pandemic years, highlighting the systemic nature of the problem.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


Evolution of Article 21 –

• Article 21 of the Constitution of India declares that “No person
  shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except
  according to procedure established by law.”

• During the Constituent Assembly debates, members were divided on
  whether to use the phrase "procedure established by law" or the
  American concept of "due process of law."

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• In A.K. Gopalan (1950) , the Supreme Court adopted a narrow
  view, holding that "procedure established by law" means any law
  enacted by the state, regardless of its fairness.

• The Court ruled that as long as a law exists, a person can be
  deprived of life or liberty, and the judiciary cannot question its
  reasonableness.

• It also held that Articles 19 and 21 operate in "water-tight
  compartments," severely limiting personal liberty.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• R.C. Cooper v. Union of India(1970) (11-judge bench) departed
  from Gopalan, holding that the word "law" in Article 21 must be
  valid and not violate other fundamental rights.

• Kharak Singh v. State of U.P. (1962) interpreted "life" to
  mean more than mere animal existence, laying the foundation
  for a broader understanding of personal liberty.

• The Court struck down domiciliary visits by police as a violation of
  personal liberty but held that the right to privacy is not explicitly
  guaranteed under the Constitution.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruled Gopalan, establishing that
  procedures under Article 21 must be "just, fair, and reasonable."

• The Court held that the right to life includes the right to live
  with human dignity and a meaningful life.

• Golden Triangle - Articles 14, 19, and 21 are interconnected and
  must be read together, significantly expanding fundamental rights.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• The 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 21A, making free
  and compulsory education a fundamental right for children aged 6-
  14.

• In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) , a 9-judge bench
  declared the right to privacy an intrinsic part of Article 21.

• The Supreme Court has also interpreted Article 21 to include
  the right to digital access, recognizing that meaningful life in the
  21st century requires digital connectivity.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


Recent News –

• The case arose from the death of a 5-year-old boy who was
  struck by a tanker while walking to school with his father.

• The landmark judgment was delivered in the case of Maniyar Iliyaz
  @ Shaik Riyaz v. P. Ayyappan & Ors. (2026).

• The Court noted that there was neither a footpath nor a
  pedestrian crossing at the place of accident, exposing the larger
  issue of unsafe pedestrian infrastructure.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• The Court held that the right to walk is integral to Article 19(1)(d) ,
  which guarantees the right to move freely throughout the territory
  of India.

• It is also connected to Articles 19(1)(a), (b), and (c) – freedom of
  speech, assembly, and association – as walking enables their
  exercise.

• The Court linked it to Article 21, holding that safe access to
  footpaths is integral to a life of dignity and safety.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• The judgment was delivered by a bench of Justices P.S.
  Narasimha and Atul S. Chandurkar.

• Justice P.S. Narasimha authored the judgment, declaring the right
  to walk on footpaths a fundamental right.

• The Court said that violation of the right to walk on
  demarcated footpaths will entitle citizens to
  invoke constitutional and legal remedies.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• The Supreme Court struck down the High Court's order which
  had reduced the compensation awarded to the victim's father.

• The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal had granted a compensation
  of ₹7.82 lakh with interest, which the High Court reduced to ₹4.70
  lakh.

• The Supreme Court recalculated the compensation to ₹11.44
  lakh and directed that it be paid within two months.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees the right to life and
  personal liberty, which has been expansively interpreted by the
  Supreme Court to include the right to live with human dignity.

• The Supreme Court has previously recognised the right to a clean
  environment, the right to health, and the right to shelter as
  facets of Article 21.

• The Court held that the right to walk on safe footpaths is
  an essential component of a life with dignity and is thus
  protected under Article 21.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• The Supreme Court invoked Article 14 to argue that unequal
  access to safe footpaths violates the principle of equality.

• The Court held that the State has a duty to ensure that all citizens,
  regardless of their economic status, have access to safe walking
  infrastructure.

• The Court's vision is a pedestrian-first approach to road design
  and urban planning.

Right to Walk on Footpaths



• The Supreme Court broadened the picture of walking by linking it
  with India's freedom struggle, where the Act ignited many ideals.

• The Court observed that walking powered the freedom
  struggle, politics, and social reforms.

• The Court noted that Mahatma Gandhi's Dandi March – a 240-
  mile walk – was one of the most significant events in India's freedom
  struggle.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


Legal Framework –

• The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 is an exhaustive legislation
  governing vehicles and the rules of the road in India.

• The Court observed that the Act is not for protecting the right to
  walk on footpaths and only lays down infrastructure for
  vehicles.

• The Court noted that the Motor Vehicles Act is built upon "vehicle"
  as the subject of legislation, while "human" interests are
  incidental.

Right to Walk on Footpaths


• In 2017, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways notified
  the Motor Vehicles (Driving) Regulations.

• The regulations state that drivers should take special
  precautions to ensure the safety of vulnerable road users such
  as pedestrians, cyclists, and children.

• However, the Court said these regulations are just guiding
  principles and neither recognise the fundamental right to walk nor
  prioritise the right to footpath over motorised roads.

SC Status


• In Chinthada Anand v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2026), the Supreme
  Court held that SC status is restricted to Hindus, Sikhs, and
  Buddhists.

• Conversion to any other religion (e.g., Christianity or Islam) results
  in immediate loss of SC status.

• A bench of Justices P.K. Mishra and Manmohan also ruled that
  converts cannot claim protection under the SC/ST (Prevention of
  Atrocities) Act, 1989.

SC Status


What is Scheduled Caste Status? –

• Scheduled Castes (SCs) are communities recognised
  under Article 341 of the Constitution as historically subjected
  to untouchability and social disability.

• The President of India issues the Constitution (Scheduled
  Castes) Order.

• It specifies which castes are deemed Scheduled Castes for each
  State. Article 342 makes similar provision for Scheduled Tribes.

SC Status


• The President of India, after consultation with the Governor of the
  State, issues the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order for each
  State.

• The Parliament has the power to include or exclude any caste from
  the SC list through legislation.

• The list of Scheduled Castes is State-specific – a caste notified as
  SC in one State may not be SC in another.

SC Status


• Reservation in government jobs and educational institutions
  under Articles 15(4) and 16(4).

• SC Status give protection under the Scheduled Castes and
  Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

• Access to scholarships, housing schemes, and other welfare
  programmes specifically designed for SC communities.

SC Status


Background –

• The Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, was issued
  by the President under Article 341 of the Constitution.

• It identifies castes, races or tribes for categorisation as Scheduled
  Castes in each State.

• The Order was designed to address the social disability arising
  out of the practice of untouchability.

SC Status


• Clause 3 of the 1950 Order states: No person who professes a
  religion different from the Hindu, the Sikh or the Buddhist religion
  shall be deemed to be a member of a Scheduled Caste.

• The Court described this bar as "categorical and absolute" –
  admitting no exception.

• A person cannot simultaneously profess and practice a religion
  other than the specified three and claim SC membership.

SC Status


• When first enacted, the 1950 Order provided for recognising only
  Hindus as Scheduled Castes.

• The rationale was that the extreme form of discrimination
  manifested in untouchability was unique to Hindu society.

• The argument was that religions like Christianity and Islam do not
  theologically recognise caste.

SC Status


• The Order was amended in 1956 to include Dalits who had
  converted to Sikhism.

• The amendment was aided by reports of the Commission for
  Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

• Sikhism was added to the list of religions whose Dalit members were
  eligible for SC status.

SC Status


• The Order was amended in 1990 to include Dalits who had
  converted to Buddhism.

• The amendment was passed through the Scheduled Castes and
  Scheduled Tribes Orders (Amendment) Act, 1990.

• The inclusion of Buddhists, like Sikhs, was based on recognition
  that Dalit converts to these faiths continued to face social
  disability.

SC Status


National Commissions –

• Originally, Article 338 provided for a Special Officer for Scheduled
  Castes and Scheduled Tribes, appointed by the President.

• This Special Officer was tasked with investigating all matters
  relating to the safeguards provided for SCs and STs.

• The arrangement remained in place from 1950 to 1978, but was
  considered inadequate to address the growing challenges faced by
  these communities.

SC Status


• In July 1978, the Government of India established a non-
  statutory Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled
  Tribes, consisting of a Chairman and four members.

• It was chaired by Bhola Paswan Shastri.

• However, as a non-statutory body, it lacked the constitutional
  authority to effectively enforce its recommendations.

SC Status


• In 1987, the government created a Commission for the
  Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes via a resolution.

• This marked a significant step towards providing institutional backing
  for the protection of SC and ST rights.

• The commission was given statutory status, but it was still not
  a constitutional body.

SC Status


• The Constitution (65th Amendment) Act, 1990 gave
  constitutional status to the Commission.

• This led to the creation of the National Commission for
  Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (NCSCST) in 1992

• The amendment replaced the earlier single-member Special Officer
  with a multi-member Commission under Article 338.

SC Status


• The Constitution (89th Amendment) Act, 2003 separated the
  combined commission into two distinct bodies: the NCSC and
  the NCST

• This was done to ensure focused attention on the distinct issues
  faced by Scheduled Tribes, which were often overshadowed.

• The amendment inserted a new Article 338A for the NCST,
  while Article 338 was amended to deal exclusively with the NCSC.

SC Status


Judicial Interpretation –

• In C.M. Arumugam v. S. Rajgopal (1976), The Supreme Court
  recognised that caste is social, but required proof of continued
  discrimination and community acceptance to retain SC status
  after conversion.

• The Court acknowledged that caste identity could survive
  conversion if the community continued to face social disability.

• This judgment laid the foundation for a fact-based inquiry into SC
  status post-conversion.

SC Status


• In Soosai v. Union of India (1985), The Supreme Court denied
  SC status to Dalit Christians due to the lack of empirical
  evidence of discrimination against them.

• The Court held that without evidence of continued social disability, SC
  status could not be claimed.

• This judgment reinforced the exclusion of Christians from SC
  status.

SC Status


• In Punjabrao v. D.P. Meshram (1964), The Supreme Court
  interpreted the term "professes" to denote an open and public
  declaration of faith, not merely private belief.

• The emphasis is on outward manifestation through conduct,
  not just internal conviction.

• This interpretation was relied upon in the 2026 judgment to
  determine when a person "professes" a religion.

SC Status


• In K.P. Manu v. Chairman, Scrutiny Committee (2015), The
  Supreme Court examined the issue of SC status after
  conversion and the burden of proof on the claimant.

• The Court emphasised the need for strict proof of continued
  social disability.

• This case highlighted the procedural hurdles faced by converts
  seeking to reclaim SC status.

SC Status


Recent News –

• The case arose from a criminal complaint filed by a Christian
  pastor (a SC convert) under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities)
  Act.

• The Andhra Pradesh High Court had quashed the FIR, holding that
  a Christian convert could not invoke the SC/ST Act.

• The pastor appealed to the Supreme Court, which upheld the High
  Court's judgment.

SC Status


• Chinthada Anand was originally from the Madiga community – a
  notified SC in Andhra Pradesh.

• He had been serving as a pastor for over a decade, conducting
  regular Sunday prayers and preaching Christian doctrine.

• These activities constituted a clear and public profession of
  Christianity.

SC Status


• The judgment was delivered on 24 March 2026 by a bench
  of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Manmohan.

• The Court not only affirmed the quashing of criminal proceedings but
  also laid down an authoritative framework governing the impact
  of religious conversion on caste-based entitlements.

• The Court rejected the argument that caste identity by birth
  could survive conversion.

SC Status


• The appellant relied on a 1977 Andhra Pradesh government
  order extending certain benefits to SC converts.

• The Court clarified that such orders only provide "non-statutory
  concessions" like economic assistance.

• They do not extend to statutory benefits like reservation or
  protection under the SC/ST Act – central legislation cannot be diluted
  by state executive orders.

SC Status


• The Court laid down a set of "postulates" governing SC status:

 ➢ The claimant must establish membership of a notified
   caste through unimpeachable evidence.

 ➢ Conversion to a non-recognised religion leads to complete
   disqualification.

 ➢ No statutory benefit can be claimed once such disqualification
   operates.

Passage:

The 2026 G7 Summit brought together leaders of major advanced economies to
discuss global security, economic stability, artificial intelligence governance, energy
security, critical mineral supply chains, and ongoing geopolitical conflicts. The summit
took place amid continuing concerns regarding the wars in Ukraine and West Asia, as
well as debates over climate finance and reform of international institutions.

The G7 remains an influential informal grouping despite the growing economic weight
of emerging economies. Outreach countries, including India, participated in
discussions on issues requiring wider international cooperation. The summit also
highlighted efforts to reduce strategic dependence on vulnerable supply chains and
strengthen cooperation in emerging technologies.

Source: Times of India

Which country held the presidency of the G7 Summit in 2026?

B. Japan

D. Canada
ANSWER - D

A. Germany
B. Canada
C. Australia
D. Japan
ANSWER - C

A. G5
B. G6
C. G8
D. G10

2026 G7 Summit?

ANSWER - B

following:
